2 trades Astros must make this offseason after early postseason exit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Houston Astros cannot react to an early postseason exit with minor roster adjustments. After finishing 81-81 and getting swept by the Chicago White Sox in the American League Wild Card Series, Houston needs to attack its two weaknesses: its rotation and an offense lacking speed and dependable outfield production.
This is still a roster built to compete around Yordan Alvarez, Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, Jeremy Peña and Hunter Brown. However, the Astros need more than a depth starter and a platoon outfielder if they intend to make another serious run in 2027.
Houston should pursue two aggressive trades. Neither would be inexpensive, but both would address a major weakness without forcing the organization into a rebuild.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Trade for Mariners ace Logan Gilbert
Astros receive: RHP Logan Gilbert
Mariners receive: INF Xavier Neyens, RHP Ethan Pecko and OF Joseph Sullivan
Trading within the AL West would create an obvious obstacle, but Houston should still call Seattle about Gilbert. The 29-year-old is entering his final year before free agency, making him a logical trade candidate if the Mariners do not believe they can sign him to an extension.
Gilbert would give the Astros the durable frontline starter they lacked throughout 2026. He finished the season with a 12-11 record, 3.73 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 205 strikeouts across 186 innings. His career numbers are equally strong: a 3.60 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings.
Pairing Gilbert with Brown would give Houston two legitimate postseason starters and reduce pressure on a rotation ravaged by injuries. The Astros used a franchise-record 18 starters in 2026, and Brown lasted only two-thirds of an inning while allowing four runs in the decisive Wild Card loss.
Seattle would demand a premium for trading an established starter to a division rival. Neyens, Houston's No. 2 prospect, offers significant left-handed power, while Pecko supplies a near-major-league arm and Sullivan adds outfield depth.
That price would hurt a thin farm system, especially with Neyens ranked among MLB's Top 100 prospects. Still, prospects are assets, and Gilbert would address the Astros' most important weakness immediately. Houston should make the trade only with confidence that it can extend him beyond 2027.
Buy low on Jarren Duran
Astros receive: OF Jarren Duran
Red Sox receive: OF Logan Hughes and RHP Bryce Mayer
Duran's value dropped sharply during a disappointing 2026 season, creating a potential buy-low opportunity. He hit .207 with a .266 on-base percentage and .361 slugging percentage, although he still produced 20 home runs and 21 stolen bases in 151 games.
Those numbers are a significant step backward from his 2024 breakout, when he batted .285 with an .834 OPS, 21 homers and 34 steals. His combination of speed, extra-base ability and experience in left and center field would give Houston an element missing from its current lineup.
The risk is obvious. Duran struck out 165 times in 2026 and posted a .627 OPS, so Houston would be betting that a change of scenery and different hitting instruction could revive him. However, he remains under club control for two more seasons, giving the Astros time to recover value.
Boston would receive Houston's No. 3 prospect in Hughes and a pitching prospect in Mayer. Houston would keep its top prospect, Kevin Alvarez, while acquiring an athletic outfielder who could lead off, create pressure on the bases and move around defensively.
Neither trade guarantees another championship, but standing still is the greater danger. Gilbert would stabilize October pitching, while Duran would make the lineup faster and less dependent on home runs. Those are precisely the bold changes Houston needs after another brief postseason appearance.

Mariners’ Cal Raleigh, Josh Naylor undergo offseason surgery
Both are expected to be ready for spring training in 2027.
(Nick Cammett/Getty Images)
The assumptions were there during the season, the questions asked after. Monday morning came the answers as the Seattle Mariners announced the two players who struggled the most at the plate in ’26 had undergone surgeries, both performed at the University of Washington Medical Center on Oct. 3.
Cal Raliegh underwent a left shoulder acromioclavicular debridement procedure performed by Dr. Albert Gee. He is expected to be fully recovered prior to the start of spring training.
Josh Naylor required triangular fibrocartilage complex repair surgery on his right wrist which was performed by Dr. Jerry Huang. He is also expected to be fully recovered prior to the start of spring training.
For Raleigh, who also dealt with a right oblique strain that required time on the injured list, the procedure he underwent last week was essentially a shoulder cleanup. While it was clear the oblique played a part in his first-half struggles, Raleigh finished on a positive note, finishing just outside the top 40 in second half fWAR and 67th out of 164 qualified batters in OPS.
The story was different for Naylor, who was observed shaking out his right hand at the plate and wincing after some swings throughout much of the season. He too was dealing with wear and tear and it worsened as the season progressed, but he insisted on playing through.
“I think everyone plays through pain,” he told the media at his locker the final week of the season. “Everyone wants to play baseball, play at the highest level, and play at your best capability. Whether it’s 50% that day, give all your 50. Whether it’s 20, give your 20. But I don’t really like to use that as an excuse. If you’re not willing to play through pain, this is the wrong job.”
With his swing and the drop of his left hand there is little doubt there was a good amount of pain associated with playing through. The results, however, were not close to typical in terms of power with Naylor posting the eighth-worst slugging (.350) among qualified hitters and hitting just 10 home runs, which included just two coming after June 12. General manager Justin Hollander, during an appearance on Seattle Sports’ Brock and Salk, pointed to a different contribution Naylor made, however.
“Obviously, I think he dealt with some physical maladies that made it tough for him to get into his power,” he said. “I will give him credit. He found a way to get hits from May 1st on. He was one of the leaders in a hit for average in the league. He found a way to contribute to the team in a positive way, in a very Luis Arráez kind of way with a lot of hits and a lot of stolen bases and trying to do the best he could.”

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners seem likely to lose Randy Arozarena to free agency this offseason.
Those aren’t easy shoes to fill.
Arozarena has been a firm presence in the heart of the Mariners’ order for the past couple seasons. He also brings an energy and confidence that fires up the fans in the Pacific Northwest.
There really isn’t another guy quite like Arozarena out there, but if the Mariners are losing him, they have to at least consider what a replacement for him might look like.
The answer might not be out there in free agency. Instead, it might depend on Seattle’s pitching surplus to improve their roster on the hitting side of things.
Candidate to Replace Randy Arozarena
One candidate was suggested in a new article on Monday by Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller.
The player: Emmanuel Rodriguez.
Rodriguez is a young outfielder who just made his debut for the Minnesota Twins this year.
“The Twins wouldn’t want to part with either Walker Jenkins or Kaelen Culpepper, but three guys a bit lower on their prospects list could be doable—with Emmanuel Rodriguez immediately becoming a candidate to fill the Randy Arozarena-sized hole in Seattle’s outfield,” Miller writes.
This is all in the context of Miller suggesting what he calls a “realistic” offseason trade for Mariners right-handed pitcher Logan Gilbert.
The package coming to Seattle would also including pitching prospect Riley Quick and infield prospect Ben Ross.
Rodriguez would be the centerpiece, though.
Rodriguez is 23 years old and originally from the Dominican Republic.
He’s been a top-100 prospect for each of the past four years in the rankings by Baseball America, MLB Pipeline and Baseball Prospectus.
Finally, he got to the bigs with the Twins at the end of the 2026 season. He went 8-for-45 (.178) with two doubles, a triple and two home runs. He actually had a 0.7 Wins Above Replacement in just 13 games thanks to a solid early impression with his defense.
The Mariners would have Rodriguez for the next half-decade if they made this deal, so it’d be worth considering.
Giving up Gilbert would be the tough part.
Case for Trading Logan Gilbert
If the Mariners were to trade Gilbert, it’d be because they have so much pitching depth.
He’s also entering the last year of his current contract.
“Between Emerson Hancock’s breakout, Kade Anderson’s arrival and Logan Gilbert’s projected salary of $16M in his final year of arbitration eligibility, the M’s might consider trading away the ace who was their Opening Day starter in both 2025 and 2026,” Miller writes. “At any rate, this starting rotation would still be quite formidable even without Gilbert. In addition to Hancock and Anderson, Seattle has George Kirby (through 2028), Bryan Woo (through 2029) and Bryce Miller (through 2029) for another two years. Ryan Sloan is also one of the top pitching prospects in all of baseball, and he might be a factor by the end of 2027.”
It’d be easiest to make this trade for Seattle if they can comprehend exactly what they’re getting in return. If they know they replace Arozarena’s spot in the lineup with an exciting young player, that certainly helps make the case for trading Gilbert.

Why Hyphen says Mariners need to ink Logan Gilbert to extension
Mariners analyst Ryan Rowland-Smith explains why keeping the right-hander is about more than just his performance.
(Olivia Vanni/Getty Images)
The Seattle Mariners have some heavy lifting to do this offseason as they attempt to bounce back from a disappointing 2026.
In addition to a managerial search, the Mariners have a few key players set to hit free agency, namely left fielder Randy Arozarena and longtime shortstop J.P. Crawford. And beyond those the soon-to-be free agents, they could also have an interesting decision to make with starting pitcher Logan Gilbert on the horizon.
Gilbert, who has a career 3.60 ERA and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings in six big-league seasons, will be in his final year of club control in 2027 and figures to be one of the biggest names to hit free agency after that season.
Seattle has yet to come to terms on any sort of contract extension with Gilbert, and reports of any extension talks between he and the M’s have been sparse.
So, with Gilbert entering his final year of club control with the possibility that he could leave afterwards, is he a trade candidate this offseason? Mariners analyst and former MLB pitcher Ryan Rowland-Smith doesn’t think that is a route the club should go with Gilbert. During Monday’s edition of Seattle Sports’ Wyman and Bob, Rowland-Smith explained why the M’s should lock down their talented right-hander with a new deal.
Rowland-Smith pointed to the way Gilbert pitched in what was a meaningless Game 162 for the M’s in their season finale as an example of why Gilbert needs to be retained.
“You got a dude who wants to pitch in (Game) 162, and the way he came out, it was not some wave to the fans and thank you. He (brought) the same intensity (he normally would),” Rowland-Smith said. “You need him when you’ve got a Kade Anderson, Ryan Sloan and so on to say, ‘This is how we do things.'”
In that final outing of the season, Gilbert struck out eight batters over four perfect innings before allowing a leadoff walk in the fifth that ended his day.
“Many guys would just say I don’t need to pitch… just have a bullpen day,” Rowland-Smith said. “Do you know how many guys I’ve played with who would do that? Do not get rid of Logan Gilbert – 1,000%.”
The 29-year-old Gilbert was one of just 13 pitchers to strike out 200 batters this season. He was also one of just five to do so while pitching at least 180 innings. The Stetson product has pitched at least 180 innings in four of his five full seasons in the majors, with the lone exception being in 2025 when he made the only trip to the injured list in his career.
“Pay the man. Have him here for a long time because he is so valuable,” Rowland-Smith said. “Logan Gilbert, sometimes I take him for granted. He’s, again, in the clubhouse and in that dugout, he is gold with some of these young players who you plan to bring up.”

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.
--Field Level Media

Atlanta Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. (shin) is starting in right field and is batting second against the visiting Cincinnati Reds and right-hander Brady Singer on Thursday, per MLB.com. Acuna fouled a ball off his left shin in Tuesday's game against the Reds and did not start on Wednesday, but he is back for the series finale and should be returned to all starting fantasy lineups against Singer. In just five career at-bats against Senger, Acuna is hitting .600 with a solo home run. The 28-year-old former MVP and five-time All-Star had two separate stints on the injured list this year with hamstring injuries, which has limited his overall production for fantasy managers. Acuna has hit .259 (102-for-394) with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, 20 stolen bases, and 60 runs scored. Braves fans can breathe a sigh of relief that they did not lose Acuna just before the start of the playoffs next week, and they will be hoping he can carry over his hot hitting in September. In 19 games during the month, he has gone 25-for-74 (.338) with seven homers and 19 RBI in 81 plate appearances.--Keith Hernandez

Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 4:14 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder) threw a bullpen session that consisted of around 30 pitches on Thursday, as expected, according to Matt Gelb of The Athletic. Luzardo said the session went well. item.content:encoded:
What are we supposed to do with Paul Skenes? Through June of this season, he was just about the best young pitcher we'd seen since Dwight Gooden 40 years ago. But over his past 15 starts, he has a 5.06 ERA, with declining velocity to go along with mediocre (at best) production.
My typical inclination is to give Skenes the benefit of the doubt. Sure, I wouldn't want to rank him as a top-three SP like I was coming into the season, but given the much longer track record of him as one of the best pitchers in baseball, he deserves some benefit of the doubt, right?
I think so. I certainly won't rank him as if he's a 5.00-plus ERA pitcher. But man, it just doesn't feel like this is a normal slump. Skenes admitted to tweaking his mechanics throughout the season to try to rediscover his old form, and nothing seems to have helped much. He had a stretch in August where it looked like he might be figuring things out, but then he allowed five runs in his most recent start last week against the Royals of all teams. He has one start with more than five strikeouts in his past seven starts and just six with more than six strikeouts since his season took that turn in late June. He hasn't looked like an impact pitcher for an awfully long time.
And, honestly, the fact that both Skenes and the Pirates have maintained he is healthy throughout this whole stretch doesn't even make me feel better. If Skenes was battling through some kind of lingering-but-manageable injury, I could at least move forward with the hope that a fully healthy offseason would get him back on track. But this? A complete collapse without a good explanation – I don't buy the World Baseball Classic as a cause for why Skenes suddenly stopped pitching well three months after making two starts there, sorry – is a lot harder to make sense of.
Players typically don't just stop being good at 25 years old without an injury, but that's less true of pitchers, certainly. What makes pitchers so frustrating is that they often do just stop being good seemingly overnight; the other side of that coin, of course, is that sometimes pitchers just start being really good seemingly overnight. I can't dismiss Skenes' sudden dropoff quite as easily as I can someone like Vladimir Guerrero's, even though both are plenty concerning.
I haven't finished my pitcher rankings yet – keep an eye out for my first batch of rankings for 2027 next week! – but there's no way I can rank Skenes as a top-12 option at this point. Top 24 seems possible, but at this point, I'm leaning toward dropping him a bit below that. Taking such action could be a huge mistake, and a huge win for anyone who does take the risk on Skenes bouncing back. But right now, I'm not ready to make that bet.
The toughest players to rank at starting pitcher
Garrett Crochet, Red Sox
Woof, that's a big one up top. Crochet was a consensus top-three starting pitcher entering the season, then struggled for a month, went on the IL with shoulder inflammation, and still hasn't returned after suffering an additional lat injury. At this point, it seems like we'll see him in the postseason, though likely only as a reliever. That, frankly, won't tell us much about what to expect from the quality of his stuff as a starter in 2027, nor about his ability to actually stay on the mound, regardless of how effective he will be.
Crochet is unquestionably one of the most talented pitchers in baseball, a massive lefty with a funky delivery and a deep arsenal full of unhittable stuff. He's shown the ability to adapt his arsenal and improve both across and within seasons. He has even shown the ability to hold up to an ace workload—exactly one time in nearly a decade, dating back to college.
And there's the issue. Even if he's dominant this postseason and healthy next spring, does that tell us anything about his ability to stay healthy? Of course not. Any price for Crochet will be a calculated risk. If you draft him as the seventh pitcher off the board, there's room for significant upside; if you draft him 47th, it could be a totally wasted pick. The specific injury Crochet has been dealing with isn't the kind we typically associate with ruining a pitcher's career – this isn't a blown elbow or some structural shoulder issue that requires surgery – but it might be the precursor to all that. Or it might not be.
The uncertainty here, combined with the upside, makes Crochet maybe the toughest pitcher to evaluate for 2027. With that said, no matter where I end up ranking him, I don't think anything we see from him this postseason could move him up in the rankings, short of him emerging as an ace starter again.
Logan Gilbert, Mariners
Gilbert just hasn't seemed quite right all season, but it's not like anything specifically looks wrong. When you go pitch-by-pitch in his arsenal, everything mostly still looks good, with four different pitches with a 30% whiff rate or better, plus an above-average whiff rate on the four-seamer and pretty good results on balls in play. The four-seamer, splitter, slider, and changeup all rate out well by Stuff+, to the point where he actually has the best overall Stuff+ rating of his career, while still rating out well by command.
But his walk rate is up to a career-high mark, his strikeout rate has regressed from his career-best mark in 2025, and he's having as much trouble with homers as ever. It's hard to put your finger on exactly why things have gone wrong for Gilbert, but they undeniably have, resulting in his worst run-prevention marks since his rookie season. My theory is that Gilbert's reintroduction of his cutter and changeup this season has just messed with his feel enough to throw him off-center a bit. Not enough to immediately jump out as a glaring problem, but enough that he hasn't been quite the same guy as the innings have accumulated.
Gilbert is a tinkerer, and he plays in an organization that encourages tinkering, which is no small part of why he has emerged as such a good pitcher in the first place. But I strongly believe in the idea that pitchers can tinker their way out of greatness just as much as they can tinker their way to it, and that's my theory for what's happened with Gilbert. The good news is that the talent still looks intact, and that should be the most important thing. Gilbert and the Mariners will surely spend the offseason trying to figure out exactly why things went wrong and how to fix it, and I'm not going to give up on a pitcher this talented. He still has top-five upside and I'm interested in buying the dip in 2027 if he falls outside of the top 12.
Jesus Luzardo, Phillies
Luzardo was so close to making it through two straight seasons without injuries. Then he started feeling soreness in his left shoulder following a complete-game shutout against the Braves on Sept. 7 and hasn't pitched since. He has been cleared to throw, however, and hasn't even been ruled out for the NL Wild Card series next week, as an MRI showed no structural damage. So, we're kind of in a holding pattern with Luzardo, and it would be really nice to see him look like himself during a deep playoff run. That won't preclude the possibility of injuries derailing his 2027, of course, but it would at least be a sign that the injury is as minor as the team has said it is.
When he was on the mound, Luzardo was better than ever and almost certainly would have established a new career-high in innings – heck, he might have even gotten to 200 innings for the first time. He pitched right to his peripherals nearly across the board and was one of the best strikeout pitchers in baseball. He was a true ace and might have been ranked as a top-five SP in 2027 without the injury concerns. As it stands, you probably can't justify a top-12 price, but it'll be tough to take him outside of the top 24, too.
Whether you'll actually be able to pull the trigger at that price will depend on your personal risk tolerance.
Zack Wheeler, Phillies
For a few weeks there, it looked like Wheeler's age and last year's surgery caught up to him all at once. His velocity crashed scarily in one start and he struggled to the tune of 23 runs in 24.1 innings of work, with the nadir coming on Aug. 24 when he gave up eight runs to the Mariners.
And then he just … fixed it. Beginning with an Aug. 30 start against the Angels, Wheeler hasn't allowed more than three runs in five straight starts, putting up a 1.71 ERA over his past five starts with 40 strikeouts to nine walks in 31.2 innings of work, which is basically exactly how he was pitching before that month-long hiccup immediately preceding it. That doesn't mean there are no concerns about Wheeler, or that we can totally ignore the downside he showed, especially at his age. But he's up to 156 innings with a 3.06 ERA and a 30% strikeout rate for the season.
That's not quite as good as he was before the injury, when he was a consensus top-five SP, and it's probably unfair to expect him to get back to that level again. His stuff isn't quite that good anymore, and it's hard to totally overcome that with pitchability and veteran guile. But you can largely overcome it, and Wheeler has done exactly that. I can't guarantee he won't just lose it entirely this offseason, but with how good he's been under extremely difficult circumstances this season, I don't think it makes much sense to doubt him at this point, either. He probably has to be ranked as a top-12 SP for 2027, despite the red flags and concerns.
Eury Perez, Marlins
It looked like Perez was finally figuring it out. In a 13-start stretch from May 22 through Aug. 22, Perez put up a 1.67 ERA and 0.90 WHIP, with a 28% strikeout rate and 8.4% walk rate, putting most of his biggest flaws throughout his MLB career behind him. That he did this despite missing nearly a month with a hamstring injury (and returning without a real rehab assignment) made it all the more impressive. Perez has long had ace-level upside, and we figured that once it clicked, it would click for good.
Not so much. He has stumbled badly toward the finish line, putting up a 9.67 ERA over his past six appearances (five starts), with his control completely abandoning him (13% walk rate) and his homer issues coming back in a big way. This doesn't mean Perez can't be an ace – maybe he's just running out of steam amid a 30-plus inning jump from 2025 to a new career high of 150 and counting. But it does mean that he hasn't totally figured it out, and that's frustrating for a player with so much talent. He had a 4.25 ERA last season, which we chalked up to rustiness coming back from Tommy John surgery, but he heads into his final start with a 4.14 ERA and the peripherals to back it up.
Of course, Perez will still be just 23 on Opening Day and still has incredible stuff, and we saw how good he can be when it does click in. You can't draft him as if he's figured it out, but I don't think it makes sense to rank him as if he's just the sum of his final numbers this season. He's too talented for that, and he absolutely could be one of the five best pitchers in baseball if he figures it out for a whole season. I'm leaning toward ranking Perez as a top-24 SP for 2027, even if it makes me a bit uncomfortable.
Jared Jones, Pirates
All aboard the Jared Jones hype train! The Pirates have finally taken the restrictors off him and he has responded with the best run of his career, putting up a 1.08 ERA with 35 strikeouts to just four walks in 25 innings during September after a seven-inning, one-hit gem against the Cardinals Tuesday night. Jones has long carried significant promise, but has rarely put together the kind of stretch that did anything more than tantalize and frustrate. And, honestly, it's possible this stretch will turn out to be nothing more than another tantalizing one before another series of frustrating ones. In fact, I'd probably bet on that being the case.
But know this: Jared Jones is going to be drafted as if this stretch is real. I saw Lance Brozdowski, whose analysis I highly respect, say he thinks Jones "should land as a top-20 arm" for 2027 in his newsletter this week, and he won't be alone. Jones has the raw stuff to be an ace – his fastball plays inconsistently because of its shape, but 98 mph is 98 mph, you know – and his control has actually been pretty good this season. That's especially true lately, but a 7.7% walk rate will play anywhere, especially with a near 30% strikeout rate.
Jones obviously has the talent to live up to a top-20 SP price, but I don't think I'll be the one to actually rank him that way. I can definitely see the case for it, but I need a stronger track record before I make that kind of pick. And Jones doesn't have it. Yet.
Logan Webb, Giants
Webb has always been a pretty weird pitcher. I've compared him to Framber Valdez in the past, in that he's an innings-eating, groundball type of ace, but he also shares a seemingly inherent inconsistency with Valdez, too. The final run prevention numbers have been pretty consistent over the years for Webb (before 2026, at least), but the way he got there would change from one year to the next, best exemplified by how he went from a 20.5% strikeout rate in 2024 to a 26.2% mark in 2025. The strikeout rate regressed in 2026, but his control remained nearly as good. He struggled through his worst full season ever, finishing with a 4.3 ERA in just 160.2 innings.
The most troubling thing is that Webb's groundball rate fell to 50.7%, still a very high mark, but also his worst since an eight-game stint as a rookie in 2019. There wasn't a sudden drop in velocity or change in his arm slot we can point to, and his sinker looked about as effective as ever, with a 2-degree average launch angle and .300 wOBA allowed. The biggest change appears to be in his pitch mix, as Webb's sinker usage ticked down in favor of more four-seamers and cutters. Those aren't even bad pitches for him, necessarily, but increasing their usage seems to fundamentally change something about Webb's profile in a way that doesn't work for him. It doesn't help that his sweeper was significantly less effective, dropping to a 24% whiff rate from 29% in 2025.
None of the changes for Webb look irreversible. He's gone through these stretches every season when he loses the feel for one pitch or another for a while, but he usually gets it back. I feel pretty good about his chances of getting the sweeper back and bouncing back in 2027, but the ceiling isn't so high for Webb that the bounce-back potential is worth overlooking the downside we just saw in action. I wouldn't be surprised if he drops down to around 40 in SP ADP, and I'll probably only rank him a little higher than that myself.

Across 182 innings (31 starts) in 2026, Seattle Mariners starting pitcher Logan Gilbert has recorded a 12-11 record with a 3.81 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 197 strikeouts. While Gilbert has still been a very useful pitcher for fantasy managers, he hasn't been quite as dominant this season as he has been in his peak years. After posting a 32.3% strikeout rate in 2025, Gilbert's strikeout rate has fallen to 26.7% in 2026. The 29-year-old's numbers have taken a considerable hit lately, as he's posted a 6.65 ERA across 21 2/3 innings in September. Surrendering the long ball has been a major issue for Gilbert in the second half of the season. Across 56 1/3 innings (10 starts) since the beginning of August, Gilbert has allowed 14 home runs (2.20 HR/9). Heading into his final scheduled start of 2026 against the Los Angeles Angels on Sunday, fantasy managers may want to temper expectations for the usually dependable Gilbert.--Will Brady

When the Detroit Tigers signed Framber Valdez back in February, right before spring training started, they were hoping he was going to give them durability in the starting rotation behind ace Tarik Skubal. Unfortunately, things didn't go as planned in terms of wins and losses for the Tigers, who traded Skubal at the trade deadline to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Valdez, however, has been as good as Detroit had hoped he would be in terms of durability this season. With Casey Mize was also traded at the deadline to the San Diego Padres, Valdez took over as the de facto ace for the rest of the season and maybe going into next season.
He made what could have been his final start of the 2026 season against the Washington Nationals at Comerica Park on Wednesday afternoon. After he threw his first pitch in the game, he joined some select company, despite lasting just 5.1 innings.
Tigers Pitcher Framber Valdez Joins Select Company
Valdez started well, retiring the first nine Nationals he faced before he ran into trouble in the sixth inning. However, Wednesday marked his 31st start of the season and according to the Detroit News' Chris McCosky, Valdez joined Kevin Gausman, Aaron Nola and Logan Gilbert as the only pitchers that have matched that number of starts in the same time span.
Against Washington on Wednesday, Valdez allowed four hits, two earned runs, walked three and struck out six before being lifted by Hinch. He faced 22 batters and threw 87 pitches. At this point in the season and with Detroit out of the postseason picture, there was no need to push him further on a cool day in the Motor City.
The 32-year-old Valdez had a lot of issues inside the Houston Astros clubhouse and with teammates on the field, but what can't be denied is his durability. The only season when Valdez failed to reach 31 starts was 2024, but he still made 28 starts and went 15-7 with a 2.91 ERA. Valdez finished seventh in the Cy Young voting that season, which was won by Skubal.
There are some big decisions facing the Tigers' front office this season and one of them will be how they are going to go about rebuilding their rotation. Sure, Skubal could come back, but that seems like a dream at this point. There is also the looming lockout this winter, which could create more delays in decisions, but building a rotation around Valdez is something that Detroit needs to do. One thing they can count on with the left-hander is durability, something that was on display this season.
Scott Roche has covered both college and professional sports for nearly three decades for various outlets. Scott has covered the MLB, NHL, and college sports and he is someone always looking for a good rumor, no matter which sport it is.

The Seattle Mariners were my World Series pick entering the year — that's how good I thought they'd be. Even if others weren't quite as high on them, there was every reason to believe this team could run away with a weak AL West. But that never came close to happening; in fact, just a year after making it to Game 7 of the ALCS, the Mariners will finish the 2026 campaign with a losing record and will miss the playoffs despite the American League being as weak as it's been at any point in recent memory.
Given how poorly this season went, major changes must be made to get this Mariners team back on track. Those changes begin with letting certain individuals depart after the year, starting with the most obvious one of all: manager Dan Wilson.
Manager Dan Wilson
Blaming the manager for things that have gone awry is often the easy way out, but what else can we do? On paper, the Mariners have one of the most loaded rosters in the sport, yet it feels like just about everyone has underperformed. Sure, a lot of the blame should be placed on the likes of Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodriguez, George Kirby and others who didn't do their jobs, but if everyone is failing to live up to expectations, there has to be something else going on, no?
Even if not, Wilson's lineup and bullpen management have been highly suspect dating back to his refusal to use Andres Munoz in the biggest moment of last year's ALCS decider. Wilson isn't the only reason why the Mariners are where they are, but he certainly hasn't helped them either. Again, major changes must be made, and the easiest move to start with would be letting Wilson go.
OF Taylor Ward
One move the Mariners tried to make to jumpstart their offense was trading for Taylor Ward, who, despite a down year in the power department, had an impressive .383 on-base percentage with the Baltimore Orioles prior to the trade deadline. Ward was drawing tons of walks and was essentially brought in as a table-setter for the likes of Randy Arozarena and Dominic Canzone. Unfortunately, Ward has been one of the worst hitters in the sport since the trade, going 9-for-85 (.106 BA) with one extra-base hit and no home runs. Ward's 15 wRC+ since the deadline ranks 269th out of 270 position players with at least 90 plate appearances in that span.
It's honestly a bit surprising that Ward hasn't been DFA'd to this point, but given the fact that he's a free agent after the year, it'd be stunning if Seattle even considered bringing him back. Sometimes, fits just don't work out as hoped, and this is one of those examples.
OF Victor Robles
Speaking of disappointing right-handed outfielders, what about Victor Robles? Not too long ago the Mariners had seemingly unlocked the best in Robles, who was one of their best players down the stretch of the 2024 campaign, but 2025 was a lost year for him, and 2026 went just as poorly.
Robles is slashing .256/.315/.308 with zero home runs in 65 games. Despite receiving 149 plate appearances, he has a grand total of five extra-base hits. Robles is still a decent defensive outfielder and offers a lot of speed, but he has a sub-.700 OPS against lefties and just hasn't hit enough to justify keeping around, even with one more year of club control.
SS/3B J.P. Crawford
J.P. Crawford is wrapping up his eighth season with the Mariners, and he's been a linchpin at the top of their lineup for most of those years. Crawford has always drawn a ton of walks, and his 13.3 percent walk rate this season places him in the 93rd percentile according to Baseball Savant. Unfortunately, Crawford doesn't hit for a very high average, doesn't hit for much power, doesn't offer much speed and is arguably the worst defensive shortstop in the sport.
For those reasons, is he really worth bringing back? Colt Emerson did struggle in his first taste of big-league action, but he was considered one of the best prospects in the sport and received a hefty pre-debut extension from the Mariners for a reason. He should be the shortstop on Opening Day 2027, and while Crawford could technically slide over to the hot corner, the team would benefit from finding an offensive upgrade at that position. Crawford was a great Mariner, but letting him walk in free agency feels like an easy choice.
RHP Bryce Miller
The Mariners considered trading either Bryce Miller or George Kirby at the trade deadline in their pursuit of adding a big bat to their lineup, and while they wound up settling on a rather Luis Castillo deal instead, there's no reason to believe talks won't heat up again this winter. At the end of the day, Seattle needs a game-changing bat, and they have a ton of pitching to offer up.
Logan Gilbert and Bryan Woo, their best starters, should be untouchable. The same goes for top prospect Kade Anderson. Kirby could get dealt, but his impeccable command makes him hard to part with. The Mariners could trade a Minor Leaguer like Ryan Sloan, but his upside is so massive that they'd probably shy away from doing so. That makes Miller, a pitcher with three more years of cheap club control and a very high ceiling, the likeliest choice to go. The Mariners shouldn't want to trade Miller, but given the free agent market's lack of high-end options and their starting pitching depth, a Miller trade for a middle-of-the-order bat makes too much sense.
OF Randy Arozarena
Randy Arozarena is one of the few Mariners players who actually surpassed expectations this season. He's slashing .279/.379/.480 with 26 home runs, 76 RBI and 24 stolen bases entering Wednesday's action. He's even scored an AL-leading 106 runs, which, given Seattle's brutal offense behind him, is pretty impressive. He's a player the Mariners should want back, but will he actually be back?
Arozarena is set to hit the open market this offseason, and with the kind of year he's had, he might be the best position player on the market. That reality will likely result in Arozarena receiving a ton of interest on the open market, and are we sure the Mariners will be outbidding teams in major markets? Letting Arozarena go would be an incredibly disappointing outcome, but the likely one nonetheless. The trade market is likely where they'll pursue their big bat.

By LUKE OLSON Associated Press
SEATTLE (AP) — Yordan Alvarez resumed his Triple Crown push with a home run and three RBIs as the Houston Astros beat the Seattle Mariners 7-0 on Tuesday night to pull even with Texas atop the AL West.
Houston snapped a three-game skid and tied the Rangers at 78-79 following their 6-3 loss to the New York Mets at home. Both teams have five games remaining, and the Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Seattle (73-84) is on the brink of playoff elimination, one season after winning the AL West for the first time in 24 years and coming within one victory of the franchise’s first World Series appearance.
Alvarez hit a two-run drive to right field in the eighth inning to tie Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays for the American League lead with 41 homers. Alvarez is first in batting average at .314 and he has 102 RBIs, six behind Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso for most in the AL.
Miguel Cabrera of the Detroit Tigers in 2012 was the most recent hitter to win a Triple Crown by leading his league in all three of those statistical categories.
Alvarez hit an RBI single in the first to reach 100 RBIs for the second time in his career. Christian Walker belted a three-run homer to make it 4-0 in the third, and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot in the sixth.
It was the 200th home run of Walker’s career and his 26th this season.
Cam Smith snapped an 0-for-26 skid with a double.
Houston starter Cristian Javier was removed after two innings with right groin tightness. He threw 45 pitches. Miguel Ullola (1-0) followed with two innings of one-hit ball for his first major league win.
Bennett Sousa, AJ Blubaugh and Logan VanWey completed the four-hitter.
Mariners starter Logan Gilbert (12-11) lasted only four innings, yielding four runs on 10 hits — the most hits he’s allowed in a game this season.
Up next
Rookie right-hander Ethan Pecko (1-0, 3.77 ERA) makes his fifth major league start Wednesday for Houston against Seattle RHP George Kirby (9-11, 4.24).

SEATTLE (AP) — Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez gained some ground Tuesday night in his chase for a Triple Crown.
He still has plenty of work to do this week.
The AL MVP front-runner went 2 for 4 with his 41st home run and three RBIs in the Astros' 7-0 win over the Seattle Mariners. Alvarez hit an RBI single in the first inning, was intentionally walked in the second and then belted a 386-foot homer in the eighth with a 109.5 mph exit velocity.
“At this point, I keep wondering why guys are pitching to him,” Houston first baseman Christian Walker said. “He just seems to come through in every moment. He's dangerous at the plate right now.”
Alvarez, who is quiet and shows little emotion, orchestrated a team meeting after the Astros (78-79) were swept by Atlanta on Sunday, squandering their lead in the AL West. His performance on Tuesday was much-needed to put Houston in a tie with the Texas Rangers atop the division with five games left this season.
“He's been backing it up all year,” Astros manager Joe Espada said.
Alvarez's two-run shot to right field tied him with Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays for the American League lead with 41 homers. Alvarez is first in batting average at .314 — five points ahead of Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson — and he has 102 RBIs, six behind Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso for most in the AL.
Alonso drove in three runs with two homers Monday against Toronto, but the teams were rained out Tuesday in Baltimore because of bad weather. They are scheduled to play a split doubleheader Wednesday.
Alvarez has six homers since Aug. 1, and the 29-year-old designated hitter has eight RBIs over 17 games in September. He'll need more to become baseball’s first Triple Crown winner since Miguel Cabrera in 2012.
Alvarez leads the AL in slugging percentage (.601), OPS (1.032), total bases (329) and walks (106). Logan Gilbert intentionally walked Alvarez in the second inning Tuesday, which was the 33rd time for Alvarez this season, already a franchise record.
It’s been a historic season for the four-time All-Star after he was limited to 48 games in 2025 because of a broken hand and an ankle injury.
If he wins the AL MVP award, the Cuban slugger will join Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers as the only players to win an MVP award while primarily serving as a designated hitter. Othani was close to winning a Triple Crown in 2024 after leading the NL in homers (50) and RBIs (130), but his .310 average fell just short to Luis Arráez’s .314.

Yordan Alvarez normally lets his bat do the talking.
But after the Houston Astros were swept in a three-game home series over the weekend by National League East champion Atlanta, Alvarez felt compelled to speak up at a players’ meeting.
“Basically for us, it was three slaps in the face they gave us right in front of our fans, especially,” Alvarez said through an interpreter. “Just use (Monday’s off day) to take it as a reset day and rest, and then the only thing left is to go out there and win the six games we have left.”
The Astros (77-79), who have lost 10 of their past 14 games, enter a two-game series Tuesday at Seattle one game behind Texas in the American League West race. They’ll complete the regular season with four games against the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif.
Alvarez has held up his end of the bargain. The MVP front-runner leads the AL with a .313 batting average and ranks second in home runs (40) and RBIs (99) as he chases a Triple Crown.
Teammate Taylor Trammell said Alvarez’s words carried weight.
“He doesn’t talk much and when he speaks, there’s a presence,” Trammell said. “This was not a ‘hoorah’ or anything like that. It’s just like, ‘Hey guys, Easy. Just be easy with it,’ and hearing it from him, it means something. You see the way he’s played all year and you can’t tell me there hasn’t been any nicks or bangs for him. And he’s going out there every single day and being the best hitter in the game right now. That’s what he’s doing. And so when he says something and he talks, you listen.”
The Astros, who missed the playoffs on a tiebreaker last season to end an eight-year stretch of postseason appearances, hold the tiebreaker over Texas after winning the season series. The Rangers have three home games against the New York Mets and three games at Minnesota remaining.
The defending AL West champion Mariners (73-83) are five games behind Texas and dropped the season series to the Rangers, leaving them essentially one game from elimination.
They staved that off Sunday as rookie Kade Anderson pitched seven scoreless innings of three-hit ball, with no walks and seven strikeouts, in a 2-1 victory at Colorado.
“You just show up and … keep going,” Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh said. “That’s really all you can do. It’s frustrating, but we made our bed, and we’ve got to lay in it. And it’s our job to show up, play hard and put our best foot forward. It’s baseball, so you never know. Just keep fighting, keep battling, try to win one pitch at a time, and you know the rest is what it is.”
Tuesday’s series opener is set to feature a pair of right-handers, the Astros’ Cristian Javier (2-6, 5.31 ERA) and the Mariners’ Logan Gilbert (12-10, 3.69).
Javier suffered a 5-2 loss to visiting Kansas City last Wednesday, despite allowing just two runs over 5 1/3 innings. He’s 3-2 with a 2.87 ERA in nine career appearances against Seattle, including six starts.
Gilbert is coming off a 2-1 loss last Tuesday to the Angels in Anaheim, Calif., despite a quality start of six innings with two runs allowed. He’s 7-4 with a 3.18 ERA in 15 career starts against the Astros. Gilbert was the winning pitcher in a 6-1 victory April 12 in Seattle as he allowed one run on four hits over seven innings, with one walk and seven strikeouts.
–Field Level Media

Hello and welcome to the final installment of our weekly two-start pitcher article for the 2026 MLB season.
If your fantasy league is still playing this week, then every inning matters. You know where you stand in each and every category, and grinding out every additional win or strikeout could be the difference between winning and losing at this stage. The pickups that are made this week could be what sets you apart from your competition.
This is a living document, so we’ll update the options below as the weekend moves along.
Before we get into it, we’ll start with a couple of notes on situations that may be unresolved or teams that may not have a two-start pitcher lined up for the upcoming week. With teams setting their rotations for the postseason, there are also pitchers who may be held back from making their projected second start, which is definitely something to keep in mind.
⚾️ Baseball is back! MLB returns to NBC and Peacock in 2026! In addition to becoming the exclusive home of Sunday Night Baseball, NBC Sports will broadcast MLB Sunday Leadoff, “Opening Day” and Labor Day primetime games, the first round of the MLB Draft, the entire Wild Card round of the postseason, and much more.
The Dodgers continue to roll with a six-man rotation and will also be interested in setting up their rotation for the postseason, so with only six games on the schedule it’s highly unlikely that any of their starters are going to pitch twice. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the ball on Monday and it’s possible that he may get an inning or two on Sunday if someone else (Blake Snell maybe) gets skipped during the week, but he should be locked into lineups regardless of whether it’s one start or two, so there’s no actionable takeaways there.
The Brewers have also been utilizing a six-man rotation for most of the second half and with six games on their docket, it’s unlikely that any of their starters get a two-start week. Jacob Misiorowski is scheduled to start on Monday against the Phillies and it’s possible he could throw a few innings on Sunday as well if the Brewers want him to get the work in. He’s in all fantasy lineups no matter what though, so that wouldn’t change anything.
The Twins have been utilizing a six-man alignment as well down the stretch, so with six games on their schedule that means that everyone will just take the ball once. Bailey Ober is pitching on Monday and would be the beneficiary if any of their other starters were to get skipped during the week, but as of now that seems unlikely. He would make for a decent streaming option though with matchups against the Giants in San Francisco and against the Rangers at home.
The Mets are also rolling with a six-man rotation to end the season, so there are no two-start pitchers there either. Sean Manaea pitches on Tuesday (at Rangers) and could conceivably pitch on Sunday as well (at Nationals) if anyone gets skipped during the week. We’ll update here if anything happens to change.
Someone on the Yankees is likely to make two starts next week, we just aren’t sure whether it’ll be Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon. Both are scheduled to pitch in Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays and both would be on regular rest for the regular season finale against the Orioles on Sunday. It’s also possible that the Yankees mix in a bullpen game there and no one winds up with the two-start week. If we gain any clarity from Yankees’ skipper Aaron Boone over the weekend, we’ll update here.
Very similar to the Yankees’ situation, we don’t have a clear picture on what the Rays will do with their rotation next week. It looks like Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen are lined up for the two games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Yankees. One of them could end up pitching again on Sunday and give them a two-start week, but that’ll all depend on how the club plans to structure its rotation for the postseason. Rasmussen should be locked into lineups regardless and Martinez is still a decent option even if it’s just a single-start week.
The Blue Jays’ rotation is extremely short-handed at the moment, leading to much uncertainty on what they will do over the final week of the season. My best guess would be another bullpen day on Monday, and then if the team is still in the mix for a wild card on Sunday, you could see Max Scherzer draw a second start for the week. It’s a gamble for sure if you want to chance that he makes two starts, but it’s one that could wind up paying off.
The Nationals also plan to utilize a six-man rotation over the final week of the season, so none of their underwhelming options are going to wind up making two starts. Unless it was Cade Cavalli though, fantasy managers shouldn’t have interest anyways.
Going Twice…
Note: Probable pitchers as of September 18 and are subject to change.
American League
▶ Strong Plays
Logan Gilbert, Mariners, RHP (vs. Astros, vs. Angels)
While it has been a disappointing season overall for the Mariners in 2026, Gilbert has certainly done his job, posting a 3.69 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and a 194/46 K/BB ratio over 178 innings through his first 30 starts. That’s right in line with what expectations were for the right-hander coming into the season. He’ll look to finish the year strong with a pair of home matchups against familiar divisional foes that he has had all sorts of success against. In a week where the quality two-start options are quite limited, Gilbert represents one of the best overall plays on the board.
Drew Anderson, Tigers, RHP (vs. Nationals, vs. Pirates)
Drew Anderson has pitched very well since joining the Tigers’ rotation in early August, registering a 2.58 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and a 31/19 K/BB ratio over 38 1/3 innings. He draws a pair of really nice matchups to finish the season with both starts coming in the spacious confines of Comerica Park. I know that he’s hard to trust given the limited track record stateside, but Anderson actually makes for a very strong play this week and is someone that I’d start in all formats.
Jake Bennett, Red Sox, LHP (vs. Guardians, vs. Cubs)
Bennett has done a really nice job in his rookie campaign for the Red Sox, compiling a 3.78 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and a 90/20 K/BB ratio across 109 2/3 innings in his 19 starts. His performance has dropped off considerably in the second half though as he seems to be hitting a bit of a wall from a workload perspective. Since July 22 he holds a 5.14 ERA and a 1.32 WHIP over 56 frames. What has still been there is the strikeouts. He has punched out six or more batters in five of his last six starts. If you’re able to absorb the ratio risk and need to make up ground in strikeouts, he’s a strong option this week.
▶ Decent Plays
Cristian Javier, Astros, RHP (at Mariners, at Athletics)
As you can expect after such a long layoff, we have seen plenty of inconsistency in Javier’s performance this season. He appears to have shaken off the rust though and is rounding into form now. Over his last three starts, the 29-year-old hurler holds a 2.20 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and a 15/7 K/BB ratio over 16 1/3 innings of work. That’s enough for me to give him a shot in a two-start week against two familiar divisional foes. Having to pitch at Sutter Health Park to finish the week isn’t ideal, but the A’s offense is limping to the finish line and there aren’t any left-handed bats there that we should be worried about. I’d feel comfortable streaming him in all league sizes.
Daniel Lynch IV, Royals, LHP (vs. White Sox, vs. Guardians)
Lynch has struggled with the transition back to being a full-time starter after spending most of the season in the bullpen. In his first eight starts he holds an uninspiring 5.28 ERA and a 17/11 K/BB ratio over 30 2/3 innings. That’s not helpful at all for fantasy purposes. He has pitched better lately though, allowing just two runs over 10 innings in his last two starts while notching victories in both of them. He gets the opportunity to play spoiler against a pair of divisional rivals this week and the added intensity of those games should lead to quality results. I’d definitely be streaming him in 15-teamers and I may even take the plunge in 12’s if I needed another viable arm.
Shane Baz, Orioles, RHP (vs. Blue Jays, at Yankees)
Baz’s first season with the Orioles can definitely be characterized as a disappointment. He enters the final week of the season with an atrocious 6-15 record, 4.11 ERA and a 1.35 WHIP over 173 innings with just 152 strikeouts along the way. He has been way more hurtful than helpful for fantasy purposes. You should expect more of the same over his final two starts. He could give you 8-10 strikeouts with a chance at a victory, but it’ll likely come at the expense of a poor WHIP and an ERA that isn’t going to be helpful. If that still sounds appealing to you, go ahead and roll the dice.
MacKenzie Gore, Rangers, LHP (vs. Mets, at Twins)
Gore has had another extremely inconsistent season, leading to a disappointing 4.67 ERA, 1.3 WHIP and a 172/69 K/BB ratio over 165 2/3 innings in 32 starts. Even the strikeouts have disappeared lately, with just three in total over 11 innings in his last three starts. It’s possible that the dropoff in production has been due to the heavy workload, in which case, there’s no real reason to expect him to bounce back in a two-start week here. The matchups are good though and in some leagues the 6-8 strikeouts that he’s able to provide here could wind up being the difference at the end of the season.
▶ At Your Own Risk
Foster Griffin, Guardians, LHP (at Red Sox, at Royals)
While Griffin has been a breakout star in 2026 and one of the best waiver wire finds of the season, he has not been the same pitcher since joining the Guardians at the trade deadline and shouldn’t be blindly started in the final week of the season. Over eight starts since the trade he holds a miserable 5.79 ERA, 1.61 WHIP and a 35/15 K/BB ratio across 37 1/3 innings of work. It’s possible that he fixes whatever has been ailing him and gets back on track this week, but the more likely scenario is continued ratio damage. Perhaps the strikeouts and the shot at a victory are worth the trade off, but think twice before locking him into lineups this week.
Yusei Kikuchi, Angels, LHP (at Athletics, at Mariners)
Kikuchi has had a rough season overall, registering a 5.02 ERA and 1.55 WHIP across 57 1/3 innings through his first 12 starts sandwiched around a trip to the injured list. He has also notched just one victory on the year. His performance has been slightly improved since returning from the injured list and he’ll try to finish the season on a high note against two divisional foes. I’m not thrilled about the prospects of using him at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento, as his long balls woes could lead to a disastrous outing there. I’d only start Kikuchi if I was desperate to make up ground in strikeouts and could afford the hit to my ratios.
Anthony Kay, White Sox, LHP (at Royals, vs. Rockies)
On the surface, a pair of matchups at the Royals and against the Rockies would normally make anyone a strong streaming candidate – especially in the final week of the season. There are some serious red flags to consider here though. Kay has really struggled down the stretch, with a 7.06 ERA over 21 2/3 innings in his last five starts. He also hasn’t completed five innings in any of those outings, and with there being a strong chance that the White Sox will need Sunday’s game to keep their playoff hopes alive, they won’t hesitate to go to the bullpen in that one either. He’s an extremely volatile play this week. He could wind up delivering eight strikeouts and a victory with solid ratios. He could wind up giving you six innings total with three strikeouts and awful ratios. It’s up to your risk tolerance whether you want to take the chance or not.
Brady Basso, Athletics, LHP (vs. Angels, vs. Astros)
Basso has been transitioning to the Athletics’ starting rotation down the stretch, but he has yet to work deeper than four innings in any game so far and is very unlikely to pitch deep enough to earn a victory in either of these starts. The overall results on the season have been mediocre at best and his limited strikeout ability isn’t attractive for streaming purposes. Unless your ratios can’t be impacted by poor performance and you’re desperate for a live body to try to pick up a couple of strikeouts, Basso is best left on the waiver wire.
National League
▶ Strong Plays
Jared Jones, Pirates, RHP (vs. Cardinals, at Tigers)
After shaking off a bit of rust in his return from the injured list, Jones has been terrific for the Pirates and for fantasy managers. Over his last 13 starts, he holds a 3.56 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and an 84/22 K/BB ratio over 65 2/3 innings – and that includes an eight-run debacle against the Mets. He has allowed three earned runs or fewer in each of those 12 other starts. He gets a nice draw for the final week and represents one of the stronger overall options on the board. He should be started in all leagues without question.
Zack Wheeler, Phillies, RHP (vs. Brewers, vs. Rays)
Wheeler is tentatively lined up to start twice next week, though if seeding for the Wild Card is already decided by Sunday, it’s very likely that he’ll get skipped or work in a very limited capacity as the Phillies structure their rotation how they want to for the postseason. That means it’s probable that he’ll only get a single start against the Brewers this week. He’s a strong option and should be started for fantasy leagues regardless, just be aware that he’s probably not going to end up making two starts.
Kevin Gausman, Cubs, RHP (vs. Marlins, at Red Sox)
The Cubs may wind up needing Sunday’s game for seeding purposes, but they’ll have already clinched a postseason berth and will want to align their rotation for the Wild Card series, so it’s possible that Gausman doesn’t wind up making that second start or is limited if he does. He’s still a quality option for the week as he starts off with a strong matchup at home against the Marlins and would be in most fantasy lineups regardless. Just understand that he may not end up making two starts.
▶ Decent Plays
Michael Soroka, Diamondbacks, RHP (at Rockies, at Padres)
If anyone is going to make two starts for the Diamondbacks in the final week of the season, it looks like it’s going to be Soroka. It’s not an easy draw though, as he has to battle the Rockies at Coors Field to start the week before finishing up with the Padres in San Diego. He has pitched well overall on the season and is coming off of a strong start against the Marlins his last time out. You can’t count on the ratios being as strong as they have been given the matchups, but the strikeouts and chances of earning a victory are still there. He makes for a solid streaming option in the season’s final week.
Robbie Ray, Padres, LHP (at Dodgers, vs. Diamondbacks)
As of now, Ray is lined up to make two starts next week, though his availability on Sunday will ultimately be determined by how the Padres choose to line up their rotation for the Wild Card series. Meaning he may end up with just a one-start week against the Dodgers in Los Angeles which is far from ideal. He’s probably still worth using, just understand that he probably doesn’t get two starts and his overall ceiling for the week is greatly diminished.
Andre Pallante, Cardinals, RHP (at Pirates, vs. Brewers)
To the shock and dismay of most fantasy prognosticators, Pallante has actually had himself a nice season in the Cardinals’ rotation, posting a 3.70 ERA, 1.26 WHIP and a 104/47 K/BB ratio over 151 innings while picking up 12 victories. He’s coming off of a brutal start against the Giants though where he was rocked for six runs on eight hits over his five frames. The matchup against the Pirates to start the week looks strong and he could be facing a Brewers’ squad missing most of its regulars on the final day of the season. As long as you keep your expectations in check, he’s a fine streaming option.
Janson Junk, Marlins, RHP (at Cubs, vs. Braves)
Junk has done a nice job logging innings for the Marlins this season, but he hasn’t been very helpful for fantasy purposes, registering a mediocre 4.50 ERA, 1.34 WHIP and a 78/31 K/BB ratio over 114 innings of work. He now has to finish the season battling two of the stronger offenses in the National League, which is most definitely not a recipe for success. He’s also not a big strikeout guy, so if you’re trying to climb in that category, there are probably better options on the board for the ratio hit you could take here. He has a higher floor than most doubles available on the waiver wire if you just need a handful of strikeouts and an outside shot at a win.
Blade Tidwell, Giants, RHP (vs. Twins, vs. Dodgers)
Tidwell has made 16 appearances (eight starts) for the Giants this season, logging a 4.56 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and a 42/21 K/BB ratio over 53 1/3 innings. What he has on his side this week is the strong likelihood that he’ll actually make two starts, and the second one against the Dodgers could come against a bunch of backups on the final day of the season. If you need seven strikeouts, decent ratios and an outside shot at a win, he’s probably worth a shot in deeper mixed and NL-only formats.
▶ At Your Own Risk
Andrew Abbott, Reds, LHP (at Braves, at Blue Jays)
Abbott has really struggled down the stretch for the Reds, compiling a 9.15 ERA over 19 2/3 innings in his last five starts. When he’s on his game, he is able to pile up strikeouts and is a threat to win, but he has not been in that form consistently in quite some time. The matchups are also tough, batting two potential playoff teams on the road. Once again, if your only concern is strikeouts and wins and you are alright taking on the ratio risk, you can fire away. If you care about your ratios at all though, I’d sit this one out.
JR Ritchie, Braves, RHP (vs. Reds, at Marlins)
With AJ Smith-Shawver getting moved back to the bullpen, it looks like JR Ritchie gets an opportunity to close out the season in the Braves’ rotation. His first start back did not go well, giving up six runs over 4 2/3 innings against the Cubs at Wrigley Field. The matchups are a bit better this week, but it’s not enough to trust him if you still have to protect your ratios. If all you’re trying to do is gain ground in wins and strikeouts and you need the volume, go ahead.
Mason Adams, Rockies, RHP (vs. Diamondbacks, at White Sox)
Never Rockies. There’s just no reason to do it, especially in a split week. Adams also hasn’t pitched well this season, posting a 5.09 ERA and 1.65 WHIP over 23 innings in his five starts. The only part that’s mildly appealing is the 23 punchouts. If you are unable to gain or lose ground in ratios and only care about moving up in strikeouts and wins (unlikely here), then you could look to him as a streaming option.
